checks.title: The root account has MFA enabled

verify.pass_when_text: AccountMFAEnabled is 1: the root account has an active MFA device.

vanta.test: MFA is enabled on the root account

steps: Sign in to the AWS console as the root user (account email and password).
Open the account menu (top right) and go to Security credentials.
Under Multi-factor authentication (MFA), choose Assign MFA device.
Choose the device type. For this check an authenticator app is enough; for Drata 225 a hardware key is needed (see IAM-002).
Register the device with two consecutive codes and confirm.
Store the recovery access in a shared, protected place of the team (not in the repo or in a chat).
remediation.notes: The AWS CLI cannot enable MFA for root: it can only be done from the console as the root user.

checks.title: The root account uses hardware MFA

verify.pass_when_text: Root has MFA and no virtual MFA device assigned to root (security key or hardware token).

drata.name: Hardware MFA for AWS Root Account

steps: Sign in to the AWS console as the root user.
Go to Security credentials and, under Multi-factor authentication (MFA), choose Assign MFA device.
Choose Passkey or security key (or Hardware TOTP token) and register the team's physical key.
Once the key is registered, remove the virtual MFA device from root (Remove) so that it is not left assigned.
In IAM > Users > MFA devices, delete the orphaned virtual registrations, which also make the test fail.
remediation.notes: Drata 225 fails with virtual MFA (authenticator app). Some auditors accept virtual MFA, but the automatic test does not. Keep at least two keys in case one is lost.

checks.title: The root account has no access keys

verify.pass_when_text: AccountAccessKeysPresent is 0: root has no access keys.

vanta.test: The root account has no access key

steps: Sign in to the AWS console as the root user.
Open Security credentials and look at the Access keys section: note the last use of each key.
Confirm that no application or pipeline uses that key; if any does, migrate it to an IAM role first.
Choose Make inactive for each key and wait a few days in case something breaks.
Choose Delete to delete the keys permanently.
remediation.notes: Root access keys give full control of the account and cannot be restricted with policies. Root keys are deleted from the console, as the root user.

checks.title: The root user is not used to sign in (at most 1 ConsoleLogin in 7 days)

verify.pass_when_text: Root has at most 1 ConsoleLogin (failed ones included) in the last 7 days, adding up all enabled regions (a sign-in through a regional endpoint is recorded in that region). API use by root is not counted.

steps: Identify who signed in as root (CloudTrail > Event history, filter by User name = root).
Give that person their own administrative access with IAM Identity Center (or an IAM role with MFA) so that root is not used again.
Reserve root only for the tasks that require it (closing the account, changing the support plan) and log them.
Create an EventBridge or CloudWatch alarm that notifies through SNS every time root is used.
Wait for the sign-ins to leave the 7-day window so that the test turns green again.
remediation.notes: Drata 124 fails with 2 or more root login attempts (even failed ones) in a rolling 7 days. The check looks at all enabled regions: AWS records the global sign-in in us-east-1 and a login through a regional endpoint is recorded in that region, so those of all of them are added up.

checks.title: IAM users with a console password have MFA

verify.pass_when_text: Every user with password_enabled = true has mfa_active = true in the credential report.

vanta.test: MFA is enabled for IAM users with console passwords

steps: Ask user {resource_id} to sign in and go to Security credentials > Assign MFA device (authenticator app or security key).
If they cannot, an administrator registers it from IAM > Users > {resource_id} > Security credentials > Assign MFA device.
If the user no longer needs the console, remove the access: Security credentials > Console access > Disable.
For users who will be migrated to IAM Identity Center, enforce MFA there instead of in IAM (see IAM-017).
remediation.notes: The credential report can take up to 4 hours to reflect the change; Drata syncs it overnight.

checks.title: The password policy requires at least 14 characters

verify.pass_when_text: MinimumPasswordLength is 14 or more. Without a custom policy (NoSuchEntity) it fails.

vanta.test: Password policy requires a minimum length of 14 or more

steps: Read the current password policy (first block, read-only): the change replaces it entirely and must not be applied without having seen it.

Generate the merged values (second block, applies nothing): length and reuse are raised only if the current ones are below 14 and 24, the four complexity requirements are enabled, and expiration (MaxPasswordAge, HardExpiry) and the permission to change one's password are preserved.
Review password-policy-new.args and only then apply it (third block); verify with get-account-password-policy.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
# read-only: fetches the current password policy into a file and shows it. If the account has no policy, it starts from an empty one; on any other error (for example AccessDenied) it deletes the file and stops, and the following blocks cannot continue
rm -f password-policy-new.args
if aws iam get-account-password-policy --query PasswordPolicy --output json > password-policy-current.json 2> password-policy-current.err; then cat password-policy-current.json; elif grep -q NoSuchEntity password-policy-current.err; then echo '{}' > password-policy-current.json; echo "the account has no password policy: starting from an empty one"; else cat password-policy-current.err; rm -f password-policy-current.json; echo "STOPPED: could not read the current policy; do not continue"; fi

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
# applies nothing: merges with the current policy and shows the values that would be applied. Length (14) and reuse (24) are only raised if the current value is lower; the four complexity requirements are enabled; expiration (MaxPasswordAge, HardExpiry) and the permission to change one's password are preserved
rm -f password-policy-new.args
if [ ! -s password-policy-current.json ]; then echo "STOPPED: password-policy-current.json is missing; run the first block first"; else python3 -c 'import json,sys; p=json.load(open(sys.argv[1])); a=["--minimum-password-length",str(max(14,int(p.get("MinimumPasswordLength",0)))),"--password-reuse-prevention",str(max(24,int(p.get("PasswordReusePrevention",0)))),"--require-symbols","--require-numbers","--require-uppercase-characters","--require-lowercase-characters","--max-password-age",str(int(p.get("MaxPasswordAge",0))),"--hard-expiry" if p.get("HardExpiry") else "--no-hard-expiry","--allow-users-to-change-password" if p.get("AllowUsersToChangePassword",True) else "--no-allow-users-to-change-password"]; print(" ".join(a))' password-policy-current.json > password-policy-new.args && echo "would apply: aws iam update-account-password-policy $(cat password-policy-new.args)"; fi

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
# update-account-password-policy REPLACES the whole policy: apply only the merged and reviewed values (password-policy-new.args), never by hand
if [ -s password-policy-new.args ]; then aws iam update-account-password-policy $(cat password-policy-new.args); else echo "STOPPED: password-policy-new.args is missing; run the first two blocks first"; fi
remediation.notes: WARNING: update-account-password-policy REPLACES the entire password policy and whatever is not passed goes back to its AWS default (for example, expiration). That is why the fix reads the current policy (first block), preserves MaxPasswordAge, HardExpiry and the permission to change one's password, raises length and reuse only if the current ones are lower, and enables the four complexity requirements; review password-policy-new.args before the third block (if a requirement must be removed, edit it there). If the first block shows STOPPED, do not continue: no file is generated and the third block applies nothing. IAM-006 and IAM-007 are fixed with the same change: apply it only once. Existing passwords do not change; the rules apply at the next password change. The commands use python3, which CloudShell has installed.

checks.title: Active access keys are rotated within 90 days

verify.pass_when_text: No active access key is 90 days or more past its last rotation (Drata 232 fails from 90 days).

vanta.test: Access keys are rotated at least every 90 days

steps: Identify which application or pipeline uses the key of user {resource_id} (last use in the credential report and in CloudTrail).
Create a second access key (IAM > Users > {resource_id} > Security credentials > Create access key) and store it in the team's secrets manager, never in the repo or in a chat.
Update the application or pipeline to use the new key and verify that it works.
Deactivate the old key and wait a few days in case something fails.
Delete the old key once it is confirmed that nothing uses it.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
USER_NAME="{resource_id}"
OLD_KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID__"
# Step 4: deactivate the old key
aws iam update-access-key --user-name "$USER_NAME" --access-key-id "$OLD_KEY_ID" --status Inactive

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
USER_NAME="{resource_id}"
OLD_KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID__"
# Step 5: only after verifying that nothing uses the key (irreversible)
aws iam delete-access-key --user-name "$USER_NAME" --access-key-id "$OLD_KEY_ID"
remediation.notes: If the application still uses the old key, deactivating it breaks the application: update the application first, then deactivate. If the user is a person, it is better to move them to IAM Identity Center instead of rotating long-lived keys (IAM-017).

checks.title: There are no active credentials unused for more than 45 days

verify.pass_when_text: No active password or access key has gone more than 45 days without being used (a never-used credential counts from its creation).

vanta.test: Unused credentials are disabled after 45 days

steps: Check in the credential report which credential of user {resource_id} has gone more than 45 days without use (password or access key).
If it is an access key, deactivate it with the command below.
If it is the console password, disable console access: IAM > Users > {resource_id} > Security credentials > Console access > Disable.
If the user no longer exists in the organization, delete it afterwards (outside this fix).
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
USER_NAME="{resource_id}"
KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_ACCESS_KEY_ID__"
aws iam update-access-key --user-name "$USER_NAME" --access-key-id "$KEY_ID" --status Inactive
remediation.notes: Deactivating a key that is still in use (for example, a monthly job) breaks that application: confirm the last use first. It can be reactivated with --status Active.

checks.title: Each IAM user has at most one active access key

verify.pass_when_text: No user has both access keys active at the same time.

vanta.test: Each IAM user has at most one active access key

steps: See which of the two keys of {resource_id} the application uses (last use in the credential report: access_key_1_last_used_date and access_key_2_last_used_date).
If the application has already been migrated to the newer key, deactivate the older one.
Wait a few days and, if there are no errors, delete the deactivated key.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
USER_NAME="{resource_id}"
OLD_KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_OLD_ACCESS_KEY_ID__"
aws iam update-access-key --user-name "$USER_NAME" --access-key-id "$OLD_KEY_ID" --status Inactive
remediation.notes: Two active keys are normal during a rotation; the check fails if they stay that way. Deactivating the wrong key breaks the application: confirm the last use of each one first.

checks.title: IAM users receive permissions only through groups

verify.pass_when_text: No IAM user has attached managed policies or inline policies: everything comes from their groups.

vanta.test: IAM users get permissions only through groups

steps: List the policies that {resource_id} has today (attached and inline) with the verification commands.
Create a group per function (for example developers) or choose an existing one, and attach those policies to it.
Add {resource_id} to the group and check that the user can still access what they need.
Remove the attached policy (detach-user-policy) or the inline one (delete-user-policy) from the user.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
USER_NAME="{resource_id}"
GROUP_NAME="__FILL_IN_GROUP__"
POLICY_ARN="__FILL_IN_POLICY_ARN__"
aws iam create-group --group-name "$GROUP_NAME"
# create-group can fail if the group already exists: that is expected. What follows is chained with && so that removing the direct permission only runs if the previous steps succeeded
aws iam attach-group-policy --group-name "$GROUP_NAME" --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" && aws iam add-user-to-group --group-name "$GROUP_NAME" --user-name "$USER_NAME" && aws iam detach-user-policy --user-name "$USER_NAME" --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
USER_NAME="{resource_id}"
INLINE_POLICY_NAME="__FILL_IN_INLINE_POLICY_NAME__"
# only after verifying that the group covers those permissions
aws iam delete-user-policy --user-name "$USER_NAME" --policy-name "$INLINE_POLICY_NAME"
remediation.notes: Removing the direct permissions before the group covers them leaves the user without access: add to the group first, remove afterwards. If the group already exists, omit create-group. An inline policy may have permissions that no managed policy covers: review its content before deleting it.

checks.title: No own policies with full administrator permissions (*:*) are attached

verify.pass_when_text: No own managed policy attached to an identity allows Action * on Resource * in its default version.

drata.name: AWS IAM Principle of Least Privilege

vanta.test: Full administrative (`*:*`) policies are not attached

steps: See which users, groups and roles have the policy attached with the verification command.
Define the permissions that are actually used (IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from CloudTrail).
Create a scoped policy and attach it to those identities.
Remove the administrator policy from each identity (detach) and check that nothing breaks.
If the policy is no longer used, delete it.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
POLICY_ARN="{resource_id}"
aws iam list-entities-for-policy --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN"

REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
POLICY_ARN="{resource_id}"
ROLE_NAME="__FILL_IN_ROLE__"
# Step 4: only after attaching the scoped policy
aws iam detach-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN"
remediation.notes: Removing full administrator without a policy that replaces it leaves those identities without access. For users use detach-user-policy and for groups detach-group-policy. AWS managed policies such as AdministratorAccess are not part of this check: in Drata they can be excluded per finding with a justification.

checks.title: Own policies do not use broad wildcards without justification (review)

verify.pass_when_text: Claude reviews the attached own policies and confirms that their wildcards (for example s3:* on a specific bucket) are scoped and justified; iam:*, or Resource * with write actions, are not.

drata.name: AWS IAM Principle of Least Privilege

steps: Read the policy with the commands below and list which wildcard actions it uses and on which resources.
Replace each wildcard with the list of actions and resources that the application actually needs.
Create a new version of the policy and check that the application keeps working.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
POLICY_ARN="__FILL_IN_POLICY_ARN__"
VERSION_ID=$(aws iam get-policy --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" --query Policy.DefaultVersionId --output text)
aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" --version-id "$VERSION_ID"
remediation.notes: This is a judgment review (Claude performs it, it is not a fixed rule): a wildcard can be acceptable. Narrowing permissions without testing breaks the application that uses them.

checks.title: A role with AWSSupportAccess exists to manage incidents with AWS Support

verify.pass_when_text: The AWSSupportAccess policy is attached to at least one role.

vanta.test: A support role exists for managing incidents with AWS Support

steps: Decide who can assume the support role (an administrators group or role) and fill in its ARN.
Create the role with a trust policy that requires MFA and attach AWSSupportAccess to it.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
TRUST='{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"__FILL_IN_PRINCIPAL_ARN__"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole","Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent":"true"}}}]}'
aws iam create-role --role-name aws-support-access --assume-role-policy-document "$TRUST"
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name aws-support-access --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AWSSupportAccess
remediation.notes: The decision is the principal that can assume the role (__FILL_IN_PRINCIPAL_ARN__). If the aws-support-access role already exists, omit create-role and only attach the policy.

checks.title: IAM Access Analyzer is active in all regions

verify.pass_when_text: Each enabled region has an ACCOUNT or ORGANIZATION analyzer in ACTIVE state.

vanta.test: IAM Access Analyzer is enabled in all regions

steps: Create an account external access analyzer in the indicated region.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer --analyzer-name external-access-analyzer --type ACCOUNT --region "$REGION"
remediation.notes: An external access analyzer has no additional cost; unused access analyzers (ACCOUNT_UNUSED_ACCESS) are charged and do not count for this check. Repeat in each region that fails.

checks.title: The account has an alternate security contact (SECURITY)

verify.pass_when_text: get-alternate-contact SECURITY returns a contact with an email. ResourceNotFoundException means there is none and it fails.

steps: Decide the name, title, email and phone of the security contact (a shared team mailbox is preferable, not a personal email).
Fill in the values and run the command.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
aws account put-alternate-contact --alternate-contact-type SECURITY --name "__FILL_IN_NAME__" --title "__FILL_IN_JOB_TITLE__" --email-address "__FILL_IN_SECURITY_EMAIL__" --phone-number "__FILL_IN_PHONE__"
remediation.notes: Who receives AWS security notices is a team decision. In accounts of an organization, a member account's contact can be managed from the management account.

checks.title: People access through IAM Identity Center instead of IAM users (informational)

verify.pass_when_text: No IAM user has a console password: people sign in through IAM Identity Center or an IdP.

steps: Enable IAM Identity Center and connect it to the team's identity provider (or use its own directory).
Create the permission sets equivalent to the permissions that {resource_id} has today.
Assign those permission sets to the person and confirm that they sign in through the access portal.
Disable the IAM user's console access and, when there is no remaining use, deactivate their access keys.
commands:
REGION="{region}"
ACCOUNT_ID="{account_id}"
USER_NAME="{resource_id}"
KEY_ID="__FILL_IN_ACCESS_KEY_ID__"
# Step 4: when the person already signs in through Identity Center
aws iam update-access-key --user-name "$USER_NAME" --access-key-id "$KEY_ID" --status Inactive
remediation.notes: It is informational: AWS recommends not using IAM users for people, but Drata and Vanta do not fail for that. The migration changes how the person signs in (new portal, new MFA): coordinate it. If the team decides to keep IAM users, document it in the access policy.
